raw_response.blind_rationale:
Blind reading of the full text (Sethy & Sahoo 2026, Discover Public Health) shows that the paper's central governance-to-WASH causal claim (Objective 3; Section 3.7, p. 9; Table 8, p. 10) estimates the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT) of active/meaningful women's participation in Village Water and Sanitation Committees (VWSCs) using propensity score matching across N = 400 rural households in 16 villages of Odisha, India, supplemented by a probit marginal effect for `VWSC awareness campaign` on consistent toilet usage (Table 5, p. 8).

1. SWiM Family Classification (`Family B` vs `none_nonfit`): Substantively, active women's participation in community VWSCs and VWSC awareness campaigns acting on water source functionality (+24.8%), household toilet usage (+19.3% in PSM; +15.8 percentage points in probit), and daily water collection time (-31.4 min) map directly onto SWiM `Family B` (assistance, participation, trust, external support), or secondarily `Family A` if local committee governance arrangements are grouped there. Excluding S149 as `none_nonfit` would ONLY be justified on one of three grounds: (a) if the extracted row in `effect_sizes.csv` captured the multidimensional Gender-WASH Inequality Index (GWII, r = -0.52, p. 9) or diarrhoeal/water-borne illness (Table 4 / Table 8) rather than a direct WASH access/functionality outcome; (b) if narrow Criterion 2 strictly excludes de facto participatory agency/attendance when no formal legal/administrative rule varies; or (c) on data-integrity grounds given severe internal reporting anomalies.

2. Narrow Criterion 2 Assessment (`borderline_governance_or_proxy` / potential `E03` flag): Although VWSCs are institutional local governance bodies under India's Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) and Swachh Bharat Mission-Gramin (SBM-G), the empirical exposure is not a legal, statutory, tariff, tenure, enforcement, or administrative rule (indeed, mandating 50% women's representation in VWSCs is proposed only as a future policy recommendation in Section 4.5b, p. 14). Instead, the paper measures a behavioural/participatory composite `Women's Agency Score (0-10)` (meeting attendance 20%, speaking time 30%, influence over decisions 30%, leadership roles 20%; p. 4) binarized at an unspecified threshold into village-level active VWSC participation, plus `VWSC awareness campaign` exposure. This is a borderline governance/participation proxy rather than a formal legal rule mechanism, warranting PI review for consistency with other Family B community-participation studies versus `E03` exclusion.

3. Criterion 4 Assessment (`yes_household_or_service_access` for functionality/usage/time; `E04` if health/GWII extracted): Table 8 and Table 5 directly measure household/community WASH service access outcomes—water source functionality, consistent toilet usage, and daily water collection time burden. However, co-reported outcomes in Tables 3, 4, 6, 7, and 8 (diarrhoea/water-borne illness, UTI/reproductive infections, MHM absenteeism, and the composite GWII index combining health, voice, privacy, and time) fail Criterion 4 (`E04`) if used as the primary extracted outcome.

4. Statistical & Reporting Quality Red Flags: (i) Severe internal outcome-label contradiction: Table 8 (p. 10) and Section 3.7 (p. 9) report ATT = +24.8% (SE = 5.2, t = 4.77, p < 0.001, 95% CI [14.6%, 35.0%]) for `Water Source Functionality` alongside +19.3% for `Toilet Usage Rate`, whereas the Abstract (p. 1) and Conclusion Objective III (p. 15) state that VWSC participation `improved toilet functionality by 24.8%`. (ii) All mathematical equations in Section 2.4-2.6 (pp. 3-5) failed to render in the published PDF (`disp lay-eq- Equa`, `inli ne-eq-IEq1`, etc.). (iii) Table 8 reports village-level VWSC treatment across only 16 villages (N = 400 households) without specifying matching covariates, propensity model, common support, caliper, balance diagnostics, agency cutoff, or cluster-robust inference for 16 villages.

raw_response.headline_estimate_summary:
1) Primary Governance/Participation Estimates — Propensity Score Matching (Table 8, PDF p. 10; text Section 3.7, PDF p. 9; N = 400 households across 16 villages; active/meaningful women's VWSC participation vs non-active villages; matching covariates, cutoff on 0-10 Women's Agency Score, and clustering adjustment not reported):
- Water Source Functionality [NOTE: labelled 'toilet functionality' in Abstract p. 1 and Conclusion p. 15]: ATT = +24.8%, SE = 5.2, t = 4.77, p < 0.001, 95% CI [14.6%, 35.0%] (beneficial access direction).
- Toilet Usage Rate: ATT = +19.3%, SE = 4.7, t = 4.11, p < 0.001, 95% CI [10.1%, 28.5%] (beneficial access direction).
- Water Collection Time: ATT = -31.4 min/day, SE = 8.6, t = -3.65, p < 0.001, 95% CI [-48.3, -14.5] (raw negative sign = beneficial reduction in daily collection burden).
- Non-C4 health/hygiene PSM outcomes in Table 8 (p. 10): Diarrhoea Incidence ATT = -12.7%, SE = 3.8, t = -3.34, p = 0.001, 95% CI [-20.2%, -5.2%]; MHM Constraints ATT = -18.2%, SE = 4.9, t = -3.71, p < 0.001, 95% CI [-27.8%, -8.6%].

2) Secondary Governance/Support Estimate — Probit Model for Consistent Toilet Usage (Table 5, PDF p. 8, N = 400, adjusted for water available at toilet, adequate privacy, regular maintenance, female education >= 8 years, and wealth index quintile):
- VWSC awareness campaign -> Consistent Toilet Usage: Marginal Effect dy/dx = 0.158 (+15.8 percentage points), Delta-method SE = 0.047, z = 3.36, p = 0.001, 95% CI [0.066, 0.250].

3) Other Non-Governance or Non-C4 Estimates:
- Bivariate correlation between Women's Agency Score and composite Gender-WASH Inequality Index (GWII, overall M0 = 0.357, Table 7, p. 9): r = -0.52 (Section 3.7, PDF p. 9; no SE/p-value printed).
- Logistic regression for Water-borne Illness (Table 4, PDF p. 7, N = 400, adjusted for poor water quality, non-functional toilet, inconsistent handwashing, child <5 years, MHM constraints, household wealth): Low Women's Agency Score Adjusted OR = 1.62, 95% CI [1.07-2.46], p = 0.023, Marginal Effect = +10.4%; Non-functional Toilet Adjusted OR = 3.21, 95% CI [2.10-4.92], p < 0.001.
- OLS regression for Water Collection Time Poverty (Table 2, PDF p. 6, N = 400, R^2 = 0.714, Adj R^2 = 0.702, adjusted for female education, wealth quintile, household size, Gajapati district): Distance to Source (km) B = 4.82, Robust SE = 0.67, t = 7.19, p < 0.001, 95% CI [3.50, 6.14], Std. B = 0.62; Handpump vs Piped B = 3.15, Robust SE = 0.89, t = 3.54, p < 0.001, 95% CI [1.40, 4.90]; Unprotected vs Piped B = 7.42, Robust SE = 1.25, t = 5.94, p < 0.001, 95% CI [4.96, 9.88].
raw_response.study_design_and_sample: Cross-sectional convergent parallel mixed-methods study conducted January–June 2023 across 4 purposively selected districts of rural Odisha, India (Mayurbhanj, Ganjam, Keonjhar, Gajapati), using multi-stage sampling (2 randomly selected blocks per district, 2 villages per block = 16 villages; systematic random sampling of 25 households per village). Primary quantitative analytic sample: N = 400 rural households (100 per district; 94.3% response rate), with N = 217 households for menstrual hygiene management (MHM) sub-analyses and 16 villages for village-level VWSC participation comparisons; complemented by 16 focus group discussions and 32 key informant interviews.
